quote.author: StephDebour
quote.name: Steph Debour
quote.text:
Five years ago, Starlink wasn't on a single ship. Now it's on 66,866. That's more ships than every provider had combined back then.

Before Starlink, if you were a sailor, your internet came from Inmarsat. An unlimited plan cost €3,259 a month for 2 Mbps, and the whole crew had to share it.

Then Starlink showed up in 2022 at US$5,000 a month for up to 350 Mbps. In 2027, a plan that covers an ullimited whole cargo ship comes in at US$4,650.

OneWeb, the closest rival in low orbit, is on 1,662 ships. Its cheapest unlimited plan is about US$7,400 a month, and it maxes out at 30 Mbps.

Market share at sea, by revenue:
2021: Inmarsat almost a third, Starlink 0%
2024: Starlink 39%, the biggest

To be fair, Inmarsat and OneWeb guarantee a minimum speed and Starlink doesn't. Some fleets still pay extra for that.

Zero to number one in four years, and still the cheaper option. That's hard to compete with.

Elon is describing the core of how neural nets (and intelligence) work: semantic compression means squeezing raw data into a compact internal model of meaning, while correlation means learning the mapping from that model to useful outputs. 

In the example, a car’s video + sensor bitstream gets compressed into an understanding of the scene, then directly correlated to the exact driving commands needed. It’s efficient single-path learning, not doing two separate things at once.

Starlink is rapidly expanding across Africa, and it has already reached more than half the continent

What started in Nigeria in 2023 has now grown into a satellite internet network spanning West, East, Central and Southern Africa

The scale today:

• 30 of Africa's 54 countries listed as having Starlink service

• Expanding into remote regions where traditional broadband infrastructure is difficult and expensive to build

And the impact goes far beyond connecting homes

In Zambia, Starlink has connected more than 600 healthcare facilities, helping medical workers access digital health systems, remote consultations and essential medical information

In Mozambique, over 300 schools have been connected, giving students and teachers access to online learning in rural communities

Across Africa, Starlink is helping connect:

• Rural homes and underserved communities
• Schools and healthcare facilities
• Farms, businesses and remote industries
• Emergency and disaster response teams
• Government services in hard-to-reach regions

For decades, connecting remote communities meant building expensive infrastructure, laying cables and extending networks over enormous distances

Starlink is changing that

A village, school or hospital no longer has to wait years for fiber infrastructure to reach it before getting access to high-speed internet

All it needs is a Starlink terminal, power and a clear view of the sky

That's what makes satellite connectivity so important for Africa's future

quote.author: SawyerMerritt
quote.name: Sawyer Merritt
quote.text:
SpaceX has agreed to forgo $738 million in U.S. federal broadband subsidies and instead provide free @Starlink hardware to eligible American households.

NTIA: "To ensure that no consumer at a Covered BSL is left behind, the provider (SpaceX) will serve the covered BSLs as this agreement provides. This includes providing customer premises equipment at no cost to new subscribers, so that households at covered BSL do not face the upfront equipment costs. Additionally, the provider’s broadband service will be subject to the same delivery timelines and performance testing requirements applicable to all recipients of BEAD funds."

Under the new agreement, SpaceX would:
• Provide free Starlink hardware to eligible households.
• Guarantee minimum download speeds of 100 Mbps and upload speeds of 20 Mbps.
• Offer a low-cost monthly internet plan.
• Commit to providing service for 10 years.
• Continue to comply with federal performance testing requirements.

The agreement will save American taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars while accelerating high-speed internet access in underserved rural communities.

In exchange, SpaceX would be exempt from most BEAD-related financial audits, procurement requirements and administrative reporting, while remaining subject to network performance testing.

quote.text: The first room at the front door was Elon‘s. There was a mattress on the floor. When the young people arrived and were dancing upstairs, I thought the floor was going to collapse so I moved the mattress to the wall. I assumed just the middle would collapse. I put the door money in a shoebox. When I saw it was quite a lot, I fetched a kitchen knife in case someone tried to take it away from me. I was also the coat check girl. posts.text:
.@TheEconomist has a piece about how AI has found many top economics papers to be formally flawed. 

I've been saying the same thing for many years, without the help of AI. 

An example is Bernoulli's bizarre error from 1738, which percolated uncorrected into the 20th century. Menger 1934 is therefore invalid (the wikipedia page on the St. Petersburg discusses his contribution uncorrected; the journal where he published his work was not interested in publishing a correction when I contacted them).

I was told way back when by economists that I seem to be right, but who cares about a 300-year-old error? 
(In the foundational work of the discipline. Well...)

How did this error travel? Kahneman and Tversky's foundational paper introducing Prospect theory seems inspired by the error. It starts by defining expected-utility theory in a mathematically implausible way. You can call it `wrong' or `erroneous' if you like. 
The weirdness goes back to Bernoulli 300 years ago, and it convinced a whole research field that humans are utterly irrational (because they don't behave as suggested by flawed formal work). 

Yes, it's a complete mess. But out of this mess grew the field of behavioral economics, with several Swedish Bank Prizes for Economic Science in Memory of Alred Nobel (the name changes every few years). 
The basis of this field is formally off. 
Over the last decade or so, economists working in behavioral economics noticed that practically nothing in their field replicates, and worse that the whole philosophy is deeply flawed -- seeing solutions to structural problems in affected people just changing their attitudes to the problems. Instead of fixing the problems.

Many of the most famous findings of the field turned out to be literally made up. Fabricated data, invented experiments that never took place.

Slowly but surely this is all coming out. Developing ergodicity economics acted as an early-warning system. We who worked on it had deep suspicions, to put it mildly, about behavioral economics.

How did this error travel? Kahneman and Tversky's foundational paper introducing Prospect theory seems inspired by the error. It starts by defining expected-utility theory in a mathematically implausible way. You can call it `wrong' or `erroneous' if you like. 
The weirdness goes back to Bernoulli 300 years ago, and it convinced a whole research field that humans are utterly irrational (because they don't behave as suggested by flawed formal work). 

Yes, it's a complete mess. But out of this mess grew the field of behavioral economics, with several Swedish Bank Prizes for Economic Science in Memory of Alred Nobel (the name changes every few years). 
The basis of this field is formally off. 
Over the last decade or so, economists working in behavioral economics noticed that practically nothing in their field replicates, and worse that the whole philosophy is deeply flawed -- seeing solutions to structural problems in affected people just changing their attitudes to the problems. Instead of fixing the problems.

Many of the most famous findings of the field turned out to be literally made up. Fabricated data, invented experiments that never took place.

Slowly but surely this is all coming out. Developing ergodicity economics acted as an early-warning system. We who worked on it had deep suspicions, to put it mildly, about behavioral economics.

quote.text:
Starlink is bringing high-speed internet to thousands of students in rural Honduras, one school at a time 🇭🇳

At Escuela Sergio Palacios in El Hatillo, 200 students now have access to Starlink internet through an installation by Conatel

And this is part of a much bigger effort to connect underserved communities

• 1,212 institutions connected through Conatel's wider connectivity program, benefiting over 167,500 students
• 1,860 Starlink antennas installed by Hondutel across 218 municipalities
• 3,100 Starlink installations planned in total
• Over 2,000 additional schools, health centers and public institutions targeted for connectivity in 2027

For students growing up in remote communities, having internet access opens up an entirely new world of opportunities to learn, research and access educational resources that were previously out of reach

This is what makes Starlink so important

When Elon Musk was a student at the University of Pennsylvania, he was paying his own way through college. He and his roommate rented a cheap ten-bedroom house that had once been a frat house and began hosting weekend parties there, charging five dollars at the door. Elon later said he could make an entire month's rent in one night, and that somebody had to stay sober to run the party, so he did. 

When Maye came to visit one weekend, she was quite surprised by it all, and then she did what Maye always does: she helped. She worked coat check and even guarded the cash, as he later joked, with a kitchen knife 😅

A reminder, for no reason in particular:

The central, profound insight of Nietzsche into irrational beliefs of groups

A group which feels unable to secure itself resources and dignity against another group, will construct a worldview that renounces and inverts the values of the two groups.

Thus irrationality on the surface is actually a defense & coping mechanism underneath.

Ressentiment

I just did this with Grok @bot and with my Amazon order history export, it found $892 I’m owed since 2017 that falls into this class action lawsuit. Crazy!

The keys to make this efficient were:

1. Get your order history exported by typing “request my data” in Amazon app search. It took 30 mins for them to email me a link to the export

2.  Download the zip and upload to @bot chat and ask it to find an email about the class action in your inbox. It was in my spam which is why never knew about it before now 🤦‍♂️ 

3. Ask it to figure out which groups you’re in and use the order history you attached to the convo, and your credit card info from the @bot Finances integration to find eligible transactions. 

4. Finally ask it to file it all for you.

Starlink helped save a young man’s life in remote Myanmar.

After a landmine blast in Kayah State, his injuries were beyond what the medic on the ground could treat alone.

Using Starlink, the team sent photos and videos to a surgeon in Germany, who guided the medic through emergency procedures. Free Burma Rangers says this helped save his life and what remained of his leg.

For remote communities with no mobile signal, Starlink can put life-saving expertise within reach, even when the surgeon is thousands of miles away.

posts.text: Starlink saves lives

quote.author: cb_doge
quote.name: DogeDesigner
quote.text:
Starlink helped rescue an injured hiker stranded in Japan’s mountains with no mobile signal. 🇯🇵

After a 6-metre fall, he was bleeding heavily, had a broken finger and could no longer walk. He used Starlink to text his wife his exact coordinates.

He spent the night under an emergency blanket before rescuers reached him around 10:30 the next morning and arranged a helicopter flight to hospital.

He says rescuers told him the coordinates he sent helped them pinpoint his location.
